papers.title: Analysis of sperm processing and cryopreservation procedures in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) to reduce fragmentation and maximize total and progressive motility
papers.abstract: The marmoset has emerged as an ideal species for studying complex neurodevelopmental diseases, and IVF is required for gene-editing success. Reliable sperm processing is paramount to several IVF techniques, including traditional insemination. If not used immediately, thermal stress from cryopreservation diminishes sperm quality, requiring improved processing methods. Swim-up and gradient methods may limit adequate sperm quality, and the lack of a standardized freezing protocol often results in impaired post-thaw motility. Thus, reliable standards for sperm processing and cryopreservation in the marmoset are needed to support vital IVF processes. Collected semen underwent one of four pre-processing incubation steps before processing by swim-up, sucrose gradient, or a microfluidics assay. Sperm parameters were assessed using a Hamilton Thorne Computer Assisted Sperm Analysis (CASA) system. To evaluate cryopreservation, microfluidics-processed sperm were subjected to five protocols using different cryoprotectants and cooling methods. After thawing, sperm samples were analyzed with the CASA system and a DNA fragmentation assay. Incubation for 30 minutes at 38C in TYH media decreased sperm aggregation, and subsequent microfluidics resulted in a higher percentage of motile and progressively motile sperm than swim-up or gradient methods. Our optimized cryopreservation protocol consistently achieved at least 20% progressive motility, a key benchmark for usable marmoset sperm, while previously published or commercial methods were less consistent. The cryopreservation protocol outperformed other published methods, having the least significant change in post-thaw motility without causing DNA damage. These findings establish standardized methods for reliably procuring and storing sperm samples for IVF or husbandry in the common marmoset.

papers.title: Cholesterol availability drives the assembly of mitochondria-associated ER membranes
papers.abstract: Mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membranes (MAM domains, or MAMs) are transient lipid raft domains of the ER that coordinate multiple cellular metabolic pathways and the ER-mitochondria communication. However, the mechanisms that drive their formation remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal that MAM assembly is dynamically regulated by the availability of plasma membrane (PM) cholesterol. We show that cholesterol delivered through high-density lipoproteins (HDLs) via the scavenger receptor class B type 1 (SR-B1) pathway is rapidly redistributed from the PM to the ER, where increased cholesterol availability promotes the assembly of MAM domains. In turn, MAM formation promotes the communication between the ER and mitochondria, the esterification of excess cholesterol and the suppression of cholesterol biosynthesis. Disruption of MAMs uncouples these responses, altering cholesterol trafficking and metabolic adaptation to extracellular cholesterol. Our findings identify MAM as a dynamic metabolic regulator that translates changes in extracellular lipoprotein availability into coordinated intracellular metabolic responses and cellular adaptation.

papers.title: Feedback control via H3K9 methylation and siRNA biogenesis autonomously maintains RNAi heterochromatin through continuous low-level transcription
papers.abstract: The logic of RNA-based silencing involves nascent RNA molecules that serve as scaffolds to recruit proteins that repress transcription. Despite transcription and silencing being antagonistic, RNA-based recruitment mechanisms have been widely adopted in organisms ranging from yeast to humans. In fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe), the nuclear RNAi pathway that establishes heterochromatin at pericentromeric repeats to silence transcription exemplifies this paradox. Current models propose that cells reconcile these opposing activities by confining pericentromeric transcription to S phase while maintaining silencing during the rest of the cell cycle. Here, using strand-specific single-molecule RNA FISH (smFISH), we detect forward and reverse pericentromeric transcripts with high sensitivity and single-cell resolution. We find that repeat-associated transcription is rare, heterogeneous and happens independently of cell-cycle control. Instead, transcript production is governed solely by feedback involving small RNA biogenesis and H3K9 methylation. By combining mathematical modeling with experiments, we show that low levels of H3K9me or siRNAs prevent heterochromatin establishment, whereas high levels of H3K9me cause stochastic switching. Our work reveals that the same RNA-based feedback architecture can sample distinct transcriptional regimes, with feedback strength determining how often cells produce transcripts without any external regulatory inputs.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics decoding of the host response to Klebsiella pneumoniae infection reveals an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis and a spatially organised inflammatory programme
papers.abstract: Background: Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp) is a leading cause of hospital and community acquired pneumonia and bacteraemia, and hypervirulent and carbapenem resistant lineages continue to expand worldwide. Although individual omics layers of Kp infection have been profiled, the host-level molecular logic that connects transcriptional, cellular, metabolic and spatial programmes has not been systematically integrated. Methods: We curated 16 public datasets spanning four modalities-bulk and dual host pathogen RNA-seq (six datasets; 118 libraries), single-cell RNA-seq (four datasets; {approx}164,000 cells), untargeted/targeted metabolomics (four datasets; 1,842 molecular features) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (two datasets; {approx}11,400 spots) covering murine lung infection models, hypervirulent and classical Kp strains, carbapenem-resistant isolates and human clinical specimens. Datasets were harmonised through a standardised pipeline (Salmon/DESeq2; Scanpy/Harmony; MetaboAnalyst; RCTD/spacexr), and integrated by WGCNA, GSVA, CellChat, Monocle3, SCENIC, joint-pathway analysis, RCTD deconvolution, and machine-learning feature selection (LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, XGBoost) with 1,000x bootstrap internal validation and independent external validation. Results: Kp infection evoked a coherent 920 gene neutrophil inflammatory response ({approx}520 up-/{approx}400 down-regulated genes) dominated by IL-17/TNF/NF-{kappa}B signalling, neutrophil degranulation, HIF-1-linked glycolysis and itaconate biosynthesis. A turquoise co-expression module (r = 0.86 with infection status) yielded a ten-gene hub signature (IRG1, S100A9, IL1B, CXCL2, SLC7A11, HMOX1, PTGS2, NFKBIA, LST1, FCGR3B). Single-cell profiling resolved twelve major lung lineages and eleven myeloid substates, tracing a Monocle3 trajectory from Cxcr2hi inflammatory neutrophils through an Irg1/Slc7a11hi oxidative phase into Cxcr4hi/Trem2hi suppressive states; CellChat identified S100A8/A9-TLR4 and CXCL2-CXCR2 as the most amplified axes (8.5x and 4.2x). Metabolomics revealed 30-fold pulmonary itaconate accumulation together with succinate and lactate elevation, glucose/glutamine depletion and glutathione collapse, and joint-pathway analysis positioned the TCA-cycle itaconate and ferroptosis modules as the strongest convergent perturbations. Spatial transcriptomics mapped these programmes onto five anatomical niches, with IRG1 expression peaking in the infection core (58% neutrophil content) and declining radially. A ten-gene host-response classification model reached AUC=0.958 in discovery, 0.937 in internal validation and 0.884-0.912 in two independent external cohorts (Brier score 0.071). Conclusions: By vertically integrating public multi-omics data, we define an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis that couples inflammatory myeloid expansion to spatially segregated metabolic niches, and we deliver a validated host-side molecular signature that discriminates Kp infection from non-infected states.

papers.title: Abundance-weighted analysis and deep functional metagenomic selection reveals unrecognized diversity of soil-derived streptothricin acetyltransferases
papers.abstract: Streptothricins (STCs) are broad-spectrum antibiotics under investigation for their therapeutic potential against antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. However, the extent and diversity of genes that confer resistance to STCs, or their environmental resistome, remains largely unknown and is essentially limited to a handful of STC acetyltransferases. Here, we used a deep functional metagenomic approach to uncover previously unrecognized STC resistance determinants. A functional metagenomic library containing ca. 700 Gigabases of soil metagenomic DNA was selected for resistance to nourseothricin (NTC), a mixture of STC congeners, resulting in collection and sequencing of nearly 30,000 resistant clones. An abundance-weighted sequence analysis identified 265 acetyltransferase-like candidates spanning broad phylogenetic, taxonomic, and genomic diversity. Re-cloning and experimental testing of 18 candidates chosen to cover acetyltransferase sequence space confirmed that 10 conferred significant NTC resistance in Escherichia coli. Phylogenetic analyses identified three previously uncharacterized STC acetyltransferase lineages, designated as SatC, SatD, and SatE. Despite substantial sequence divergence from characterized streptothricin acetyltransferases (maximum amino acid identities of approximately 31% for SatC and SatD and up to 47.5% for SatE), these enzymes largely retained key residues associated with streptothricin binding and catalysis. In addition to strongly increasing NTC resistance, expression of the SatC construct in E. coli also significantly decreased susceptibility to the aminoglycoside antibiotics amikacin and kanamycin. Together, these findings reveal a substantially broader than previously known environmental repertoire of STC acetyltransferases and demonstrate how deep functional metagenomic selections, combined with abundance-weighted hit calling, phylogenetic analysis, and structural prediction, can uncover novel resistance functions.

papers.title: Dietary fibre responses emerge through host-dietary regime interplay: Apple pectin modulates immune reactivity in adult zebrafish
papers.abstract: Dietary fibres are rarely consumed independently. Instead, they form part of an overall diet that includes dietary fibres from different sources, in varying amounts and consumed under different feeding patterns. Here, we tested how dietary regimes containing apple pectin, oat {beta}-glucan, or cellulose shaped the host. We analysed gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA sequencing, measured brain and intestinal SCFA profiles by targeted metabolomics, and assessed immunomodulation by measuring gene expression systemically in the blood and locally in the spleen, as well as intestinal enzyme activity. The dietary intervention was conducted for 12 weeks on adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Our results show that the gut microbial composition can be relatively stable across different dietary fibre exposure patterns yet still vary significantly between the sexes. Additionally, the effect of sex on the gut microbiome may become more evident when dietary fibres are administered at high dosages, but intermittently. Dietary fibre regimes can alter intestinal short-chain fatty acid profiles more readily than brain profiles, which show a stronger sexually dimorphic response. Interestingly, apple pectin modulated the zebrafish immune response through interactions dependent on the overall regime, tissue, sex, and host immune status. Notably, tissue il1b gene expression differed depending on how apple pectin was administered and the host's physiological state. Collectively, our study emphasises the highly context-specific effects of dietary fibres, shaped by the dynamic interplay between the overall dietary regime and intertwined host factors.

papers.title: Two genomes in one mitochondrion: mitochondrial heteroplasmy and mitogenome dynamics in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
papers.abstract: The mitochondrial genome of the model green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii has long been described as a 15.8-kb linear molecule capped by inverted telomeres. By leveraging high-accuracy long-read sequencing to overcome limitations associated with conventional genome algorithm biases, we demonstrated that this classical paradigm was incomplete. Our analyses provided no evidence for canonical telomeric structures, instead revealed widespread structural heteroplasmy characterized by the coexistence of two distinct mitochondrial genome configurations. In addition to the historical 15.8-kb configuration (designated as config 2), we identified an expanded 19-kb configuration (config 1) containing 4,001-bp terminal inverted repeats that duplicate the cob and nad4 genes. Single-molecule long-read profiling captured these configurations as a dynamic network of multimeric mitochondrial DNA concatemers bridged with a conserved 17-bp homologous motif. Together, these structural features support a recombination-dependent replication (RDR) model that could enable mitochondrial DNA replication in the absence of conventional telomeric structures and reverse transcriptase-like (rtl) genes. We further identify widespread nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), which complicate targeted amplification and quantification of these mitogenome configurations. Specifying NUMTs enabled configuration-specific digital PCR measurements across the CC-5325 lineage and additional field-isolated Chlamydomonas strains, revealing substantial variation in the relative abundance of the two mitogenome configurations. These findings revise a four-decade-old model of the C. reinhardtii mitogenome and provided a new framework for investigating mitochondrial genome architecture, structural heteroplasmy, and replication dynamics in photosynthetic eukaryotes.

papers.title: Pattern-triggered immunity induced by dsRNA against plant viruses involves two distinct branches, one of which depends on Coronatine insensitive1 (COI1)
papers.abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a conserved molecular signature of RNA virus generated during infection that can activate antiviral pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) in plants. However, the effectiveness of dsRNA-induced PTI against viruses from diverse taxa, its impact on different stages of the infection, as well as effectors used by viruses other than tobamoviruses to counteract this defense response remain poorly explored. Here, we established an Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression assay for inducing PTI through intracellular production of nonspecific dsRNA in Nicotiana benthamiana. Expression of nonspecific dsRNA restricted cell-to-cell movement and accumulation of three RNA viruses representing different taxonomic groups: Tobacco mosaic virus, Turnip mosaic virus, and Tobacco rattle virus. Co-expression of dsRNA together with a P25 movement protein (MP) mutant of Potato virus X (PVX) defective in RNA silencing suppression, prevented dsRNA-induced callose accumulation at plasmodesmata (PD) and restored efficient viral cell-to-cell movement. Interestingly, dsRNA also reduced viral RNA accumulation at the cellular level, revealing an impact of dsRNA-based PTI on virus replication independently of cell-to-cell movement. We further showed that the dsRNA-induced antiviral response required jasmonic acid (JA) signaling. Silencing of the JA receptor Coronatine insensitive1 (COI1) abolished dsRNA-induced PD callose deposition and the associated restriction of virus movement and accumulation. Accordingly, dsRNA-induced expression of defense-related genes was compromised in COI1-silenced plants. Next, we conducted RNA-seq analysis to identify early biological processes involved in COI1-dependent, dsRNA-induced immunity. The differential expression of 198 genes, some potentially involved in the regulation of callose accumulation, in COI1-silenced plants suggested that JA signaling contributes to shaping the transcriptional response to nonspecific dsRNA. Together, our findings establish nonspecific dsRNA-induced PTI as a multilayered antiviral response that restricts pathogen replication and cell-to-cell movement, and identify a heterologous MP, PVX P25, as an effector that counteracts the PD component of this defense response in a COI1-dependent manner.

papers.title: Compost from urban biowaste shapes the bacterial community and its functional traits in the rhizosphere of tomato plants
papers.abstract: Industrial compost derived from urban biowaste is a sustainable biofertilizer made from food waste and plant matter. It has long been used as a fertilizer in agriculture and horticulture for its rich nutrient content. However, the composition of the microbiota in industrial biowaste compost has been studied only partially, and the effects of this bacterial community on soil, rhizosphere, and plant root communities have received limited attention. In this study, we conducted community and functional analyses to examine how the microbiota in biowaste compost influences bacterial diversity, community composition, and metabolic potential in tomato plants, compared with plants fertilized with conventional, unsustainable chemical fertilizer. Source contribution analysis tracking bacterial taxa indicated a significant contribution of compost-derived taxa to the soil, rhizosphere, and roots. The community analysis revealed distinct clustering by fertilizer type, with biowaste compost promoting a unique, more diverse rhizosphere community, enriched in Firmicutes species. Functional analysis highlighted increased microbial pathways in the rhizosphere treated with biowaste compost, including enzymes for cellulolytic and xylanolytic activity, nitrogenase, phytase, and 1-ACC deaminase. Overall, food-derived industrial biowaste compost enhances bacterial diversity and the predicted functional and plant growth-promoting potential in the rhizosphere of tomato plants, underscoring its potential as a sustainable biofertilizer that supports soil health, microbial biodiversity, and crop productivity.

papers.title: Evolution of immune infiltration and immune triad formation across early melanoma progression
papers.abstract: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) in melanoma are a clinically important prognostic marker and are routinely used to inform patient care. However, when immune recognition of transformed melanocytes begins and how it evolves during early melanoma progression is not well understood. Using spatial transcriptomics and a unique cohort of patient-matched lesions representing multiple stages of early evolution, we investigate T cells, dendritic cells (DCs) and multi-cell immune "triads" during melanoma initiation. We find that T cell and DC density, triad density, and triad proximity to melanoma cells are elevated in regions of Stage I invasive melanoma as compared to Stage 0 in situ lesions and nevi. Further, we find that triad abundance correlates with both T cell and DC density, but is not predicted by clustering patterns of these cell types over larger spatial scales. We conclude that immune recognition of melanoma and engagement with the lesion significantly increases with progression from Stage 0 to Stage I disease. Further, using nevi that are depth-matched in the dermis to Stage I invasive lesions, we demonstrate this increased immune recognition is not a consequence of dermal invasion alone. This points to a paradigm where immune engagement of invasive melanoma reflects recognition of melanoma cell-intrinsic changes that emerge in Stage I disease.

papers.title: Genome-wide fluctuating selection under demographic cycling in Icelandic rock ptarmigan
papers.abstract: Understanding how natural populations adapt to continuously shifting environments is central to evolutionary biology. Multi-annual population cycles impose temporally varying selective pressures, yet disentangling the resulting genomic signals from those of sustained directional selection and genetic drift has been challenging due to a lack of high-resolution temporal data. Here we investigate the genomic consequences of demographic cycling in a population of rock ptarmigan (Lagopus muta) from northeastern Iceland. We analyzed whole-genome sequences from 91 individuals sampled over an 11-year period, encompassing two population peaks (2010 and 2018) and two troughs (2007 and 2013). Testing allele frequency change at each SNP against a null model of drift and sampling, we identified candidate loci and grouped them by correlation of their temporal trajectories. Cluster trajectories fluctuated through time, and two were closely correlated with the regional census, one significantly tracking the demographic cycle, while a smaller set changed monotonically in a manner consistent with sustained directional selection. Each cluster contained loci distributed across many chromosomes, indicative of genome-wide responses to selection. The most strongly fluctuating loci overlapped candidate genes of possible functional relevance, most notably CTNNA2 (Catenin Alpha-2), which is associated with startle response and anxiety-like behaviors and may relate to predator avoidance. Our findings indicate that fluctuating selection comprises much of the temporal genomic response in this natural population, and suggest that multi-annual demographic cycles can drive rapid and widespread allele frequency change, highlighting the value of temporal genomics for clarifying the interplay between demography and natural selection in wild populations.

papers.title: CDC25B couples ribosome biogenesis to cell cycle kinetics to promote spinal cord neurogenesis
papers.abstract: During neurogenesis, neural progenitors undergo a tightly regulated transition from proliferation to differentiation, which requires precise coordination between cell cycle progression and molecular reprogramming. Although the role of CDC25B is well established in promoting G2/M transition through CDK1 activation, we previously showed that it is both necessary and sufficient to trigger neural progenitor differentiation, via CDK-dependent and CDK-independent mechanisms. However, the molecular networks underlying this neurogenic activity remain poorly understood. Here, using a gain-of-function approach in the chicken spinal cord combined with bulk RNA sequencing, we show that CDC25B overexpression upregulates transcripts encoding ribosomal proteins and enhances ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) in neural progenitors. Consistent with these findings, during normal development, RiBi increases in neurogenic progenitor domains expressing CDC25B. Notably, the increase in RiBi is not associated with an increase in translation in neural progenitors. Instead, it is followed by an increase in mTORC1 activity in neuronal precursors and subsequently by a rise in the global translation rate in differentiating neurons. Moreover, increasing mTORC1 activity is sufficient to trigger a premature transition of neuronal precursors to the next step of differentiation. Altogether, our data support a model in which CDC25B coordinates cell cycle progression with RiBi in neurogenic progenitors, thereby initiating a program that culminates in translation in differentiating neurons.

papers.title: STRIPAK associates with Rabex5-Rabaptin5 to promote Rab5-dependent early endosome formation and EGFR transport
papers.abstract: His Domain Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase (HD-PTP) is required for multivesicular body (MVB) formation and endosome maturation, with Rab5-GTP levels raised upon HD-PTP depletion (Parkinson et al., 2021. doi: 10/1242/jcs.259192). Mass Spectrometry-based interactomics revealed that HD-PTP depletion increased association of Rabaptin5, a component of the early endosome Rabex5-Rabaptin5 Rab5-GEF, with multiple components of STRIPAK (striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase). Native IPs and co-expression studies confirmed association between STRIPAK and Rabex5-Rabaptin5, including Strip1-Rabex5 and SLMAP-Rabaptin5 interactions. Consistent with functional Rabaptin5-STRIPAK links, co-depletion of Strip1 or Rabaptin5 with HD-PTP restored normal early endosome positioning and Rab5 distribution. Strip1 depletion impaired formation of central, Rab5-positive early endosomes, reduced cellular Rab5-GTP levels, and prevented the accumulation of internalised EGF-EGFR into centrally located endosomes. SLMAP depletion accentuated the central clustering of early endosomes and other endosomal compartments while also retarding the generation of new, EGFR-containing endosomes and EGFR lysosomal transport. We conclude that STRIPAK is a novel co-assembly factor of Rabex5-Rabaptin5, exerting subunit-specific effects on early endosomes.

papers.title: Endonuclease G governs an antiviral RNA surveillance system in budding yeast
papers.abstract: Endonuclease G family DNA/RNA nucleases localize to the mitochondrial intermembrane space and prevent escape of mitochondrial DNA to the cytosol or nucleus. While extramitochondrial Endonuclease G also targets nuclear DNA during cell death, RNA regulatory roles of this family remain enigmatic. Here we discover an RNA surveillance system in Saccharomyces cerevisiae governed by Nuc1, the yeast Endonuclease G homolog. This system limits replication of L-A, an RNA mycovirus that endemically infects this organism. Whereas L-A resides in the cytosol, we find that Nuc1's antiviral function requires its mitochondrial intermembrane space localization. To understand Nuc1's indirect antiviral mechanism we investigated its genetic interactions with REX1 and REX2, RNA exonucleases that control 3' end processing of tRNA and rRNA intermediates in the nucleus. We demonstrate that the nuc1{triangleup} antiviral defect is massively amplified by rex1{triangleup} rex2{triangleup} leading to L-A RNA levels that surpass mature rRNAs and overwhelm the cells. NUC1 concurrently controls a pool of mis-processed tRNA and rRNA species that accumulate in rex1{triangleup} rex2{triangleup} mutants. Linking these mis-processed RNAs with L-A control, we show they are significantly reduced in L-A infected cells, suggesting that L-A depletes them to enhance its replication. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized RNA surveillance function of Nuc1 that prevents aberrant rRNA and tRNA species from promoting replication of the L-A mycovirus.

papers.title: A portable C-terminal rheostat calibrates RecE/Redα exonuclease activity for enhanced bacterial recombineering
papers.abstract: Recombineering enables precise genome engineering across diverse bacteria, yet efficient tools for large DNA integration remain underdeveloped for Streptomyces and other biotechnologically relevant bacteria. Here we identify a panel of highly active RecET recombinase pairs from actinobacteriophages that mediate efficient homologous recombination in Streptomyces. The lead candidate, Che9cRecET, supports genomic integration of kilobase-scale DNA with only 50bp homology arms and enables accurate insertion of 79kb biosynthetic gene clusters, far outperforming conventional genome editing approaches. Structural and biochemical analyses reveal Che9cRecE as a distinct C3-symmetric toroidal homotrimeric 5'-3' exonuclease, whose extended C-terminal loop acts as a tunable rheostat calibrating exonuclease activity to an optimal window for recombination. We further show this portable C-terminal loop enhances recombineering efficiency across phylogenetically diverse exonucleases including Escherichia coli Redalpha/RecE and Pseudomonas A. Our work uncovers a conserved regulatory mechanism of the RecE/Redalpha exonuclease family and delivers a generalizable strategy for advancing bacterial genome editing.

papers.title: A droplet-to-data workflow for antimicrobial screening of complex matrices
papers.abstract: Screening plant extracts and other complex natural matrices for antibacterial activity is complicated by optical interference and population averaging in conventional bulk assays. Droplet-based assays mitigate interference while enabling high-throughput assessment of bacterial subpopulations. However, analyzing the resulting image data involves difficult image processing, classification, and interpretation. Here, we present a democratized workflow for antimicrobial screening in complex matrices that combines a polydisperse droplet-based assay with EasyFlow 2.0 (EF2), our updated droplet image analysis platform. EF2 offers stable containerized deployment, expanded polydisperse droplet support, automated thresholding and MIC estimation, LLM-assisted data exploration, and import of other software outputs such as CellProfiler (CP) measurements and CellProfiler Analyst (CPA) classification models. As proof of concept, we applied this workflow to assess the antibacterial and aggregation-modulating effects of chemically distinct extracts of Taraxacum officinale, Rhodiola rosea, and Lonicera caerulea against Escherichia coli. Extracts were chemically characterized by HPLC-MS and evaluated using both standard 96-well plate microdilution and droplet-based assays. In total, 27,059 droplets were segmented in CP, classified into four growth phenotypes using a CPA random forest model, and analyzed in EF2. The droplet-based assay reached minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) at lower extract concentrations than 96-well plate microdilution and revealed extract-specific aggregation effects: L. caerulea reduced E. coli aggregation, whereas T. officinale did not. R. rosea reduced growth in the 96-well plate microdilution assay, but high concentrations caused droplet gelation that prevented droplet-based analysis, showing that sample components must be checked for compatibility with droplet formation. These results illustrate that the EF2-centered workflow supports rapid, automated MIC estimation through unsupervised thresholding when labels are unavailable, and four-class aggregation phenotyping when a CPA model is supplied. This workflow offers flexible, scalable screening, potentially extendable beyond plant extracts to other complex sample matrices.

papers.title: The influence of drug dosing regimen on extinction and adaptation during experimental evolution in Candida albicans
papers.abstract: The antifungal azole drug fluconazole (FLC) is frequently prescribed for treating Candida albicans infections. Azole drugs are typically fungistatic; they inhibit cell growth rather than kill susceptible cells within a population. Therefore, fungal populations can adapt to fluconazole through increased drug resistance or increased drug tolerance (the ability of a subpopulation of susceptible cells to grow slowly at inhibitory drug concentrations). To our knowledge, no prior experiments have examined how different factors influence extinction propensity, although previous in vitro studies show that both drug concentration and strain background can influence adaptation. To determine how the drug dosing regimen, namely fluconazole concentration and transfer duration (i.e., the amount of time between transfer into fresh medium), influenced extinction and adaptation in Candida albicans, we conducted a fully factorial series of short in vitro evolution experiments. Dosing regimen significantly influenced extinction: all replicates evolved at all drug concentrations survived the 48 h and 72 h transfer experiments, yet the extinction rate increased sharply from low to high drug concentration with 24 h transfers. Increases in drug tolerance were frequent regardless of the dosing regimen. In contrast, drug resistance and growth rate both tended to decrease following evolution at higher drug concentrations. Fluconazole-evolved replicates exhibited frequent increases in cross-tolerance and decreases in cross-resistance in a panel of other azole drugs. Genome size changes were common in some strain backgrounds evolved to higher fluconazole concentrations, regardless of transfer times. Combined, our results indicate that many experimental factors can influence the trajectory of adaptation, and show that extinction in a fungistatic drug occurs readily at high drug concentrations with rapid transfers.

papers.title: E. coli-produced nanobody fusions as a pan-serotype platform for AAV purification, quantification, and detection
papers.abstract: Research, production and application of the recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) require versatile tools for rapid and cost-effective advances. We developed fusion constructs with the pan-serotype, AAV-binding VHH-antibody-fragment named nanobody AAVX and devised procedures for AAV purification, quantification, and detection. Starting from an amino acid sequence, we cytosolically expressed in E. coli nanobody AAVX carrying various tags and fusion partners. Very efficient soluble production followed by a one-step immobilized metal-ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) yielded mostly >90% pure protein. Crosslinking AAVX with an agarose matrix enabled efficient purification of intact AAV2 and AAV5 capsids from cell lysates, as assessed by qPCR and ELISA. AAVX also supported effective AAV quantification by ELISA, as capture reagent and, when fused to luciferase, as detection reagent. Using tagged AAVX and streptavidin biosensors, we developed a rapid and label-free quantification assay of AAV capsids by biolayer interferometry (BLI). Finally, immunostaining with an AAVX-eGFP fusion visualized AAV capsids in fixed HEK-293 cells by fluorescence microscopy. Collectively, these results establish nanobody AAVX fusion proteins as versatile and readily customizable tools for AAV research and bioprocessing.

papers.title: Spatial expression evolution of duplicated genes post-whole genome duplication in cultivated tomato
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which whole genome duplication contributes to expression divergence of duplicate genes, which can impact the evolution of form and function, has been a long-standing question in evolutionary biology. We compared expression patterns of paralogs derived from the most recent Solanaceae-specific genome triplication event across 23 tissues and inferred ancestral expression states to investigate patterns of expression evolution. While the partitioning of ancestral expression states is traditionally considered the second most common (after the gene loss) trajectory of duplicate expression evolution, we found that the ancestral expression states tended to be retained by most (~66%) duplicates, with ~6% of gene lineages experiencing expression gain events and ~20% experiencing expression losses. The genes that gained expression in fruit tissues are significantly enriched with functions associated with fruit quality. Notably, asymmetrical expression divergence is prevalent among duplicates, especially when ancestral genes were either not expressed or were highly expressed. Our study demonstrates the utility of integrating paralog expression comparisons with phylogenetic analyses to document the potential evolutionary history of spatial expression patterns and gain insight into how expression divergence contributes to the evolution of function across tissues.

papers.title: On the asymbiotic germination of some New Zealand spider orchids (Corybas).
papers.abstract: Corybas is a large and widespread genus of terrestrial orchids, but little has been done to understand their germination. We tested germination of five species of helmet orchid (C. cheesemanii, C. dienemus, C. iridescens, C. macranthus and C. oblongus) on a range of asymbiotic media. Corybas macranthus germinated on four of seven tested media. From other species there was limited germination; for C. cheesemanii germination occurred for only two of five capsules collected concurrently and sown under the same conditions. The failure of filled seeds to germinate under optimal conditions could suggests the presence of seed dormancy. We trialed desiccation and warm moist stratification as methods to break dormancy, however this was unsuccessful.

papers.title: Identification of TM4SF1 as a novel tumor-associated antigen in biliary tract cancers targetable by CAR-T cell therapy
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are a rare set of genetically heterogenous and aggressive malignancies associated with delayed presentation and poor prognosis. Thus, there is an unmet clinical need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Identification of uniquely expressed cell-surface, tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) holds promise in epithelial tumors more generally, as they can serve as ligands for a variety of therapeutics, including CAR-T cell therapy. However, TAA identification in BTCs has been limited by expression in normal liver tissue. Here, we aim to characterize the cell-surface protein transmembrane 4 L six family member 1 (TM4SF1) as a potential BTC TAA targetable by CAR-T therapy. Methods: TM4SF1 expression in BTC relative to normal hepatic/biliary tissue was characterized at the mRNA level by analyzing TCGA datasets and at the protein level by immunohistochemistry of archival primary BTC tissue. Anti-TM4SF1 CAR-T cells were evaluated through in vitro coculture assays against human-derived BTC cell lines and in a cell line-derived xenograft (CDX) model. Results: We find TM4SF1 is significantly upregulated in BTC relative to normal hepatic/biliary tissue and across BTC anatomical subtypes at the mRNA and protein level. To validate TM4SF1 as a targetable TAA in BTC, we show anti-TM4SF1 CAR-T cells demonstrate robust growth inhibition of BTC cell lines in vitro and significant anti-tumor activity against a CDX in vivo. Conclusions: Together, our data provides support for TM4SF1 as a promising TAA in BTCs that can be used for the rational development of targeted therapeutic modalities, including CAR-T cells, in a patient population with significant unmet need.

papers.title: C19 trityl and silyl andrographolide analogs exhibit in vitro anticancer activity in murine cancer models
papers.abstract: Andrographolide, a labdane diterpenoid isolated from A. paniculata has been investigated for activity in a broad panel of biological contexts, including its anti-inflammatory, antiviral, and anticancer properties. Previously, A-ring analogs of andrographolide bearing silyl and trityl ethers at C19 have demonstrated improved in vitro anticancer activity in human cancer cell lines, with putative activity through the Wnt1/{beta}-catenin signaling axis. In order to investigate the activity of this series of C19 andrographolide analogs, alongside a cyclic A-ring acetonide analog, as anticancer agents in murine cancer cell models, we evaluated antiproliferative activity of these compounds in B16F10 melanoma, CT26 colorectal adenocarcinoma, Neuro2a neuroblastoma, and 4T1 mammary ductal carcinoma cell lines, and found that most compounds exhibited potent micromolar level anticancer activity. Among these, all trityl ethers exhibited nearly indistinguishable IC50 values of 4-20 M, and generally exhibited greater potency compared to C19 silyl ether analogs. This anticancer activity was further validated through apoptosis flow cytometry, wherein we concluded that our compounds induced apoptosis to a greater extent than the parent compound, andrographolide. Further, we examine the role of modulation of canonical Wnt1/{beta}-catenin signaling in a series of co-delivery assays with CHIR-99021, a selective GSK-3{beta} kinase inhibitor, and MSAB, a selective {beta}-catenin degrader. Finally, we demonstrate that a selection of silyl ether analogs of andrographolide elicit cell cycle arrest by flow cytometry in a manner that is decoupled to in vitro potency trends. Altogether, we report the first in vitro evaluation of trityl and silyl ether analogs of andrographolide within murine adherent cancer cells.

papers.title: Epigenetic Remodeling Increases Plasticity of Bovine Fibroblasts Without Improving Embryo and Stem Cell Development
papers.abstract: Epigenetic memory, reinforced by redundant heterochromatic networks, is a major barrier to somatic cell reprogramming. In cattle, single-agent chromatin-modifying treatments show inconsistent efficacy, likely due to compensatory crosstalk among repressive marks. Here, we evaluated a multi-target small-molecule cocktail, GUSTC, combining GSK343 (EZH2 inhibitor), UNC0638 (G9a/GLP inhibitor), Sodium Butyrate (HDAC inhibitor), Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor), and Chaetocin (SUV39H1 inhibitor) to simultaneously target facultative and constitutive heterochromatin in bovine fibroblasts. At optimized, non-cytotoxic concentrations, GUSTC treatment reduced H3K9me2, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and HP1-alpha levels while increasing H3K9 acetylation by immunofluorescence. Using GUSTC-treated fibroblasts as donor cells for somatic cell nuclear transfer did not significantly change cleavage (83.6% vs. 92.2%; p = 0.15), blastocyst rate (28.4% vs. 39.0%; p = 0.20), bovine embryonic stem cell line derivation efficiency (26.3% vs. 33.3% of seeded blastocysts; p = 0.57), or the core pluripotency marker profile (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2) of the resulting lines. In a separate, serum-free, pluripotency-permissive culture system, GUSTC-treated cells adopted a colony-like morphology and showed increased POU5F1 and NANOG expression, along with increased DNMT1, EHMT2, HDAC1, HDAC2, and SUV39H1 transcripts. GUSTC thus reduces repressive heterochromatin marks in donor fibroblasts and is associated with a potentially more reprogramming-permissive state, without detectable improvement in preimplantation developmental competence. It provides a starting point for chemical reprogramming strategies in cattle.

papers.title: Anatomically matched spatial comparisons identify Trps1 as a regulator of knee interzone formation
papers.abstract: How the interzone forms and gives rise to articular cartilage, ligaments, and synovium is incompletely understood. Using our previously generated spatial and single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the mouse hindlimb, we compared the knee interzone with neighboring tissues and with the ankle interzone at matched positions, and identified Trps1 as a knee interzone-enriched candidate. Pseudotime analysis placed Trps1-high cells in a transitional state between chondrogenic progenitors and matrix-producing chondrocytes, with higher chondrogenic and lower fibroblastic program scores. Targeted Trps1 knockdown in hindlimb explants disrupted joint formation, permitted Col2a1 expression within the interzone, and reduced adjacent cartilage formation. The associated chondrogenic program was conserved in the human embryonic knee, whereas TRPS1 expression in osteoarthritic cartilage was associated with a fibroblastic matrix program. These results support a role for Trps1 in knee interzone development and show that anatomically matched spatial comparison with explant perturbation can nominate and test joint regulators.

papers.title: The Structural Basis of Genome Silencing: The Inactive X Chromosome Resolved by Electron Spectroscopic Imaging
papers.abstract: The eukaryotic nucleus has a hierarchical organization that permits genomic regulation. The genome is packaged as chromatin, which is silenced conditionally as facultative heterochromatin, or more stably silenced as constitutive heterochromatin. The smaller fractions of the genome that contain gene-rich sequences are organized into open chromatin conformations known as euchromatin. The inactive X (Xi) chromosome territory presents a uniquely powerful model system to investigate chromosome-scale gene silencing, as the entire chromosome undergoes coordinated epigenetic repression. The unique chromosome-wide silencing event provides a tractable system for investigating how molecular mechanisms of gene repression are translated into mesoscale structural features. This work builds on previous structural studies of the Xi that have leveraged conventional electron microscopy (EM) and cryo-EM, which have led to remarkable insights into the structural underpinnings of genome silencing. These approaches, however, are unable to directly distinguish chromatin from RNA and protein features. To resolve the molecular composition of the Xi chromosome territory and to provide a model of the structural organization of the chromatin, RNA and protein we analyzed the Xi using Electron Spectroscopic Imaging (ESI). We are able to resolve structural features without the use of contrast enhancing stains, using the distinct elemental signatures of chromatin, RNA and protein and combining them into composite images. By coupling ESI and electron tomography, we can circumvent the projection limitation of EM and provide an unprecedented view of the spatial organization of chromatin fibres in relation to structural features including RNA and proteins in 3D. Additionally, we employed correlative light-microscopy with ESI in physical serial sections and computationally assembled a structural model of the entire Xi chromosome territory revealing an intricate spatial network with distinct chromatin domains, distributed RNA-protein clusters, and identified a large, and previously uncharacterized mesoscale non-chromatin structure. Together, these observations provide new insights into the architecture of the Xi chromosome territory and shed electrons on the structural basis of chromosome-scale genome organization.

papers.title: Single-nucleus transcriptomics links telencephalic cell signatures to ocean acidification effects on social behaviour in a coral reef fish
papers.abstract: Mutualistic interactions are fundamental to the health and stability of reef ecosystems. While elevated CO2 has been implicated in impairments in interaction behaviours, how this environmental change alters cellular states and intercellular communication in the brain remains unresolved. Here, by analysing the single-nucleus RNA profile of ~66,000 telencephalic nuclei from a keystone mutualist, the cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus), interacting under ambient or elevated CO2 conditions, we identify highly cell type specific neural responses to elevated CO2. We highlight a substantial depletion in Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cells (OPCs), notably linked to oligodendrocyte myelination and neural structure maintenance. Elevated CO2 also elicited targeted transcriptional shifts across discrete cell types, characterised by widespread glutamatergic signalling and altered co-expression networks associated with pH regulation, energetic metabolism, and circadian rhythm, thereby compromising the cleaner's physiologic equilibrium. Additionally, cell-cell communication was altered under elevated CO2, including remodelling in SEMA4 and PTPR signalling pathways within radial glial and OPCs, respectively, revealing network signalling rewiring in response to the changed environment. These findings uncover the high-resolution neural substrates vulnerable to ocean acidification, providing mechanistic insight into how climate-driven environmental changes alter brain function and destabilise complex mutualistic ecological interactions.

papers.title: How many mutations does it take to evolve a new function?
papers.abstract: Biochemical and genetic networks in cells evolve to produce new functions. Evolution is guided by the genotype to phenotype map which describes how mutations at the molecular scale lead to changes in network function at the cellular scale. The number of genotypes is astronomically large which makes these maps very high dimensional. In this context, the simple question: How many mutations does it take to evolve a new function?, is usually hard to answer. Here we consider this question in the context of a simple Boolean-network model of a genotype-phenotype map. The nodes and edges of the Boolean network represent the genotype while the Boolean function the network computes is the phenotype. The network evolves by rewiring of its edges, while keeping the number of nodes fixed. We compute the number of mutations needed to achieve a new Boolean function as a function of the number of nodes in the network. We show that the number of mutations scales with the number of nodes of the network as a power-law with an exponent determined by local geometrical features of the genotype-phenotype map. Our theoretical study emphasizes the role of the genotype-phenotype map in determining the time to evolve a new function.

papers.title: Experimental evolution unveils a role for structural variants and sex-specificity in the genetic architecture of lifespan
papers.abstract: Insights into the genetic basis of lifespan evolution can link evolutionary theory with an understanding of health, disease and adaptation. We leverage the power of >200 generations of experimental evolution in a seed beetle to unveil the genomic architecture of lifespan evolution. Replicated populations evolved under regimes favoring either a short or long life, resulting in a near doubling of lifespan. Whole genome re-sequencing revealed that short- and long-lived lines were strongly differentiated (global FST = 0.41) and more than 700 genes showed consistent signs of divergent selection. Remarkably, short- and long-lived lines were consistently divergent in a large number of regions harboring copy-number variants (CNVs), involving >600 genes. The evolution of a long life involved many distinct biological processes, such as DNA fidelity, mitotic integrity, reproduction, metabolism, immunity and stress response. A pedigree-based genome scan for quantitative trait loci (QTLs) uncovered several QTLs with large effects on lifespan, but the genetic basis of a long life was dominated by a very large number of regions with medium and small effects. The genome-wide spatial association with QTL effects was, if anything, stronger for CNVs than for sequence variants. The genetic effects of QTLs on lifespan were positively correlated overall between the sexes, but four regions showed pronounced sex-differences. Our results show that structural variants play a significant role in the evolution of an extended lifespan and the highly polygenic genomic architecture is to some extent sex-specific, consistent with differences in physiology and life history tradeoffs between the sexes.

papers.title: Genomic Potential vs. Pathogenic Reality: Functional Virulence Variation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of bacterial genome sequencing, predicting pathogen virulence from genomic information remains a major challenge. To study this association, we integrate comparative genomics, functional phenotyping, host-pathogen interaction assays, and infection outcomes across a diverse collection of 28 Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, representing clinically relevant diversity in serotype, type IV pilus group, and flagellar type. While virulence-associated systems were broadly retained across the strain collection, isolates displayed substantial variation in phenotypic behavior and pathogenicity. Genotypic classifications based on pilus, flagellar, siderophore, or secretion system characteristics were poor predictors of virulence-associated phenotypes. Pathogenicity in a Galleria mellonella model varied markedly among strains and was most strongly associated with surface-associated motility, whereas other virulence traits and quorum-sensing genotypes showed limited predictive value. In a three-dimensional lung epithelial cell model, inflammatory responses were negatively correlated with activity of the type III secretion system effector ExoS, suggesting a role in modulation of host immune signaling. Together, these findings demonstrate that virulence emerges from functional deployment of conserved virulence repertoires, rather than their mere presence. By linking genomic diversity to phenotypic expression, pathogenicity, and host responses within a single strain collection, this study highlights fundamental limitations of gene-content-based virulence prediction and underscores the importance of integrating genomic and functional data to better understand P. aeruginosa virulence.

papers.title: Complementing Biosafety Levels With Societal Safety Levels
papers.abstract: Biosafety level (BSL) classifications of biological agents have succeeded at minimizing occupational risk inside laboratories, but largely neglect the potential for onward transmission. As a result, many non-transmissible pathogens that could kill at most one individual per person exposed require greater containment than 1918 influenza, a virus that killed 50-100 million and might cause a new pandemic today. Laboratory workers are consenting professionals; the public is not. We recommend complementing BSLs with explicit thresholds for expected societal harm. Here we formalize Societal Safety Levels (SSLs) based on expected public fatalities per year, which we quantify from (i) estimated probability of laboratory release, (ii) likelihood of societal transmission, and (iii) consequence. SSLs would apply specifically to laboratory research with replication-competent potential pandemic pathogens, and would not restrict field surveillance, sequencing, or countermeasure development using non-replicating systems or pandemic-incapable agents. We find that applying the 0.1 expected deaths per facility-year standard common across multiple major-hazard industries to potential pandemic pathogen research would require marked safety improvements. Complementing BSLs with SSLs would establish enforceable accident-safety thresholds for pandemic-capable pathogens, bringing high-risk biological research into alignment with the quantitative safety standards that help other hazardous industries operate with public acceptance.
